# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

This interdisciplinary project brings together formal and computational semantics with natural language processing (NLP). It examines how formal meaning representations can capture replacement self-repair (RSR) in natural language.

Speakers sometimes revise an utterance before they have finished it. This process is called self-repair, a type of disfluency with three parts [@shribergPreliminariesTheorySpeech1994; @leveltMonitoringSelfrepairSpeech1983]. The *reparandum* is the abandoned material. The *interregnum* is the interval between the end of the reparandum and the onset of the coming repair. It may contain an editing expression such as *I mean* [@clarkPausesHesitationsPsycholinguistic2006]. The *repair* is the material with which the speaker resumes the utterance. This project focuses on replacement self-repair (RSR) within a clause, in which the repair replaces the reparandum and changes the intended meaning.

@fig-siri-repair illustrates an RSR: the speaker begins by asking Siri about the weather in Berlin, then replaces Berlin with Dublin. In the utterance, *in Berlin* is the reparandum, *I mean* is the editing expression occupying the interregnum, and *in Dublin* is the repair. Although Dublin expresses the speaker's final intention, Siri returns the weather for Berlin.

![Siri responds to the withdrawn location, Berlin, after the speaker replaces it with Dublin.](figures/siri-b-i-d.png){#fig-siri-repair width="420px" fig-alt="Siri weather response showing Berlin after a spoken replacement from Berlin to Dublin."}

Mainstream computational approaches commonly detect the reparandum and editing expression for subsequent processing. One approach removes them while retaining the repair, producing fluent text intended to express the speaker's final intention [@johnsonTAGbasedNoisychannelModel2004]. Another retains the spoken words and marks disfluent spans or tokens [@futamiStreamingJointSpeech2023]. In the weather example, the first approach retains only *in Dublin*, while the second would preserve both cities but marks *in Berlin* as disfluent.

Explicit MRs remain useful in LLM-based systems because they make model-interpreted meaning inspectable beyond surface text. They organise entities, events and their relations into structures that can be examined formally [@bosSequenceNotationCatching2023]. In recent work, explicit MRs have been used to detect unsupported relations in generated database queries [@reganMASSIVEMultilingualAbstract2024], evaluate the contextual appropriateness of dialogue responses [@yangEmphasisingStructuredInformation2025] and construct paraphrase-resistant semantic watermarks [@yeSWANSemanticWatermarking2026]. These uses illustrate why explicit semantic structure remains useful for verification, evaluation and subsequent processing.

For applications using explicit MRs, self-repair raises the question of what information should remain after a speaker revises an utterance. The reparandum can continue to affect comprehension, as shown by psycholinguistic evidence [@lauLingeringEffectsDisfluent2005]. It may also remain available for later reference in dialogue [@purverComputationalModelsMiscommunication2018].

Returning to @fig-siri-repair, suppose the speaker receives the correct response and follows with *"Show me the airports of these two cities"*, referring to both locations. Cleaned text would retain Dublin but lose Berlin, leaving only one explicit antecedent for the plural expression *these two cities*. A transcript marked with disfluency labels would preserve both names [@futamiStreamingJointSpeech2023], but the labels would not specify how Berlin's semantic role has been revised.

Thus, I argue that an MR for RSR should encode the semantic content of the reparandum and repair, together with the structural configuration through which the utterance is revised. In the running example, both cities should be linked to the weather request, with an ordered replacement structure designating Berlin as the withdrawn location and Dublin as the accepted one. This representation keeps Berlin available for later reference while recording that Dublin has replaced it in the original role. The same distinctions make a parser's output inspectable: its errors can be traced to omitted content, incorrect status assignments or incorrect links to shared content. The project has developed a formal representation of within-clause RSR. The proposed thesis will validate its coverage and train and evaluate semantic parsers that generate it.

Simplified Box Notation (SBN) [@bosQuantificationAnnotationDiscourse2021; @bosSequenceNotationCatching2023] is a suitable starting point because it combines a structured meaning representation with a sequential format suitable for LLM generation. Its structure can be extended to distinguish withdrawn from accepted content while preserving their connections to the surrounding utterance. SBN is also used for semantic annotation in the Parallel Meaning Bank (PMB), whose existing sentence--SBN pairs provide a basis for synthesising RSR data [@abzianidzeParallelMeaningBank2017].

The proposed thesis will address two research questions.

1.  **Representation:** How should within-clause RSR be represented in SBN, and what are the coverage and limitations of the representation?

2.  **Parsing:** How well can LLM-based semantic parsers learn this representation from synthesised meaning-banked data, and what errors remain?

This thesis aims to make three contributions.

1.  A representation of within-clause RSR in SBN, together with an account of its coverage and limitations.

2.  A completed diagnostic study of how an LLM-based semantic parser trained on fluent sentence--SBN pairs processes RSR.

3.  A data-generation and training pipeline that constructs paired RSR utterances and repair-aware SBNs from meaning-banked data and trains LLM-based parsers to produce the repair-aware representation.

@sec-related-work (*Related Work*) reviews disfluency processing and semantic accounts of repair. @sec-formalism (*Formalism*) defines the repair-aware SBN. @sec-methodology (*Methodology*) presents the diagnostic pilot, corpus construction and model experiment. @sec-timeline (*Timeline*) records completed work and remaining milestones.
